chart_check: Two panels — left: bars for motorist deaths (110 in 2013, 81 in 2025 labeled) plus a red line for all road-user deaths, y "Deaths per year", rotated year labels, no cut-offs or overlaps; right: risk curve with y "Risk per mile, 2025 = % of 2013", x "Miles driven in 2025 as % of 2013", black break-even dot at (74, 100) and red dot at (100, 74), legend readable. Bars/line match values.csv; annotations check out (81/110 = 73.6% → "74", "−26%"); the green/red background shading has no label.
answer: Yes — motorist (vehicle-occupant) deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025, a 26% drop, and since the file has no miles-driven data I solved for it: per-mile risk only fails to decline if 2025 driving was below ~74% of 2013's mileage. So if 2025 miles driven are similar to 2013's, the risk of a motorist being killed per mile is ~26% lower — but the driving assumption cannot be verified from this data (as the right panel shows). Caveats: the 2020–21 spike, and post-2019 reported crashes fell 60% (211,486 → 85,546) while injuries fell far less — persons_injured −19% (61,391 → 49,634) and motorist_injured −26% (45,836 → 33,737).
